source.title: UNBIND: UNlearning By INference-time Directional Steering for Code LLMs
source.authors: Zhengyang Shan; Jia-Yu Xin; Yan-Jun Lin; Xuan-Cheng Qian; Zhi-Hong Liu; Ming-Hui Xu; Yue Zhang; Qin Hu; Kun Li; Xiu-Zhen Cheng

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling, truncation, or wrong-document issue; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests a different, inference-time representation-intervention method for code unlearning and measures its behavior under prompt and extraction conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports prompt rephrasing, target-prefix injection, and fenced-code access evaluations, but aggregates outcomes across the prompt conditions and attempts. Its own method is evaluated; results for other unlearning methods are not included here. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, direction ablation as a recovery attack, or quantization.
record.test_reason: The study proposes UNBIND, an inference-time hidden-state steering method with weights fixed, for unlearning memorised code on two 7B code models and two corpora. It reports target reproduction (F-BLEU), utility, and a fixed-budget prompt and target-prefix extraction suite against Mfull and retain-only references. These results bear on A (unlearning works, here as verbatim reproduction), E (recovery by prompting) and F (a counter-method that resists prompt attacks), in the new setting of LoRA-memorised code.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that UNBIND cuts target code reproduction by 97–99% with little utility loss and gets the best joint forgetting–utility score against 14 baselines. They also conclude that it nearly eliminates long exact-span recovery under repeated fixed-budget extraction, and that the multilingual and related-code tests show the suppression is targeted.
record.recipe_differences: UNBIND is an inference-time hidden-state intervention using a detector, a separately constructed output direction, and a calibrated gate; model and adapter weights remain fixed. It is not a post-training gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The tested access outcomes aggregate six prompt conditions and greedy/sampled attempts, so condition-specific sensitivity is not reported. UNBIND uses separately calibrated layers and settings for each model–corpus task.
record.problems: The main forgetting evaluation uses designated training targets rather than held-out forgetting generalization. The fixed-budget access results aggregate across prompt conditions and attempts, preventing condition-by-condition comparisons. The paper does not give a chance-level accuracy reference for its reproduction results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row cap. Other methods' results and component ablations were not included because they are not recovery attacks on UNBIND or measurements of the specified attack versions.

untested.parts: Knowledge-QA accuracy vs chance; only verbatim code reproduction is measured. No held-out forgetting generalisation: F-BLEU is on the 300 designated training targets, which include calibration rows (Appendix A.1). The forgotten content was memorised through the authors' LoRA adaptation, not pretraining.

No direction-ablation or hook-removal attack, and no deletion-vs-blocking analysis. By design the weights stay unchanged, so the knowledge remains in Mfull and removing the hook (Algorithm 2) would restore it; this is not measured.

No jailbreaks. No other-language prompts for the same targets: the multilingual tasks are separate forget sets with their own interventions. The six access conditions are reported only as a maximum, never per condition.

Robustness is tested only against the fixed-budget prompt and prefix suite (at most 30 completions per target). Not tested against fine-tuning, disabling the hook, direction ablation, quantisation, or white-box attacks.

missing.what: F-BLEU and utility for the 14 baselines (RMU, GA, NPO-KL, SimNPO-KL, GradDiff, GSS, etc.). These bear on A for standard unlearning methods: several reduce F-BLEU only partly (e.g. GA 0.3031 and CodeEraser 0.3872 vs 0.4847 on QwenCSN).
Access-suite results for PROD, GSS, SimNPO-KL, FLAT and Task Vector, aggregated with the original prompt. Examples: PROD QwenCSN 63/13, R 60.00; FLAT CLStack 0/0, R 0.89; GSS CLCSN 0/0, R 1.52.
Multilingual UNBIND FR/UR/FU-H for the Python, Java and JavaScript forget tasks; the authors report FR above 97% in all six settings
Related-code retention NLL (same-language and cross-language neighbours)

record.verdict_notes:
Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) The refusal was caused by two row_fixes items each for r27, r30, r33 and r36: one linked E with state absent, the other linked A and F with state observed. Each pair is now one item with versions A, E, F and state "absent". The state refers to the effect the row measures, prompt-based recovery. Each problem text says that for A and F this absence means the version holds. The labels are unchanged: A supports, E challenges, F supports, all from these rows.
(2) Added a point to those rows: the access value is a maximum over the six conditions, so it is an upper bound on every condition's span count. Per-condition breakdowns are not reported, but no single condition can show recovery above the aggregate.
(3) Added RMU's configuration (Table 6: 13 updates, λR 100/1200, layers 5–7) to the condition of the A "challenges" label, because so light an update makes under-tuning a plausible cause.
(4) Added CodeLlama baseline access numbers from Table 8 to the missing entry, and the partial-forgetting baselines to the first missing entry.
Everything else is kept.

Standing caveats:
- UNBIND is an inference-time hook with model and adapter weights unchanged, so by construction the knowledge is blocked, not deleted. Anyone with weight access gets Mfull back by removing the hook. This was not tested as an attack, but it limits F's robustness claim to black-box prompting.
- Prompt-supplied tokens are excluded from matching. Mretrain is the meaningful baseline, since it also produces some spans.
- The forgotten targets were memorised during the authors' LoRA adaptation, not pretraining.
- The baseline implementations, including RMU, are the authors' own.
- Tranche T3 (new setting); the reader's T2 stays revised.
- The text contains no instructions aimed at the reader.

versions.untested_parts: The paper evaluates code reproduction and utility, and prompt/extraction access, but does not report targeted-knowledge accuracy against a chance level.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning-set recovery attack.
No attack that ablates an activation direction to recover targets, and no test establishing that an existing unlearning method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No low-bit quantization of unlearned weights.

Tests instruction rephrasing, fenced-code prompting, and target-prefix injection; does not test jailbreaks, other-language prompts for the same forgotten targets, or in-context information beyond target-prefix injection.
Tests UNBIND against the reported fixed-budget prompt and extraction suite, not against fine-tuning, direction-ablation, or quantization attacks.
